summary.text: A varve is one year's worth of sediment, laid down as a pair of layers: one coarse and one fine.
Because each couplet stands for one year, counting them gives high-precision dates, which makes varves one of the most important records for studying past climate change.
They form only in fresh or brackish water, since sea salt clumps clay into coarse grains all year and makes the separate layers nearly impossible to tell apart.

facts.label: Word origin
facts.value: Swedish 'varv', with meanings like 'circle' and 'in layers'

facts.label: Swedish chronology
facts.value: 13,200 varve years, built from thousands of sites

items.prompt: You cut into an old lake bed and find repeating pairs of coarse and fine bands. When was the coarse band of each pair most likely washed in?

options.label: In deep winter, under the ice
In late autumn, as the lake calms
In spring, when strong flows carry bigger grains
In a dry summer, when streams shrink

items.explain: Spring brings stronger water flow, which carries much coarser particles than the gentler flow later in the year.

items.prompt: A geologist wants yearly layers to count. Why is a freshwater lake a far better place to look than the open-sea floor?

options.label: Salt clumps clay into coarse grains all year, hiding the layers
Sea floors are too deep for any sediment to settle
Ocean currents carry all the mud back onto land
Lakes freeze solid, which stops the layers mixing

items.explain: Salt water makes clay coagulate into coarse grains year-round, so there is no clear coarse-fine switch to mark each year.

items.prompt: A lake core shows 500 light-dark couplets stacked neatly with nothing missing. Roughly how long did that mud take to build up?

options.label: About 250 years
About 1,000 years
About 50 years
About 500 years

items.explain: Each couplet is one year, so 500 couplets record about 500 years.

items.prompt: On one lake floor, worms and other burrowing creatures constantly churn the mud. What would you expect to find there?

options.label: Extra-thick, very clear yearly layers
No neat yearly layers at all
Twice as many layers per year
Layers that only form in winter

items.explain: Varves need the sediment to be left undisturbed by living things; churning mixes the layers away.

items.prompt: While mapping layered lake mud in Sweden, Gerard De Geer was struck by how much it looked like another familiar natural record. Which one?

options.label: Growth lines on seashells
Bands in agate stones
Rings in tree trunks
Stripes in cave stalactites

items.explain: The resemblance to tree rings led him to suggest that each coarse-fine pair was a yearly layer.

items.prompt: In many lakes the pale summer layer is made of silica and calcium carbonate. Why does it build up mainly in warm months?

options.label: Warm water dissolves the lake bed's rocks
Summer storms blow sand in from beaches
Snowmelt floods are strongest then
Tiny organisms thrive, then their dead shells sink

items.explain: Phytoplankton and other micro-organisms with silica or calcium carbonate shells are most productive in warm months, and their remains fall to the bottom.
